## Executive Summary: Key Findings, Headline Metrics, and Regulatory Divergence

## Problem Statement

The 2026 legislative cycle marks a pivotal inflection point for Level-4 (L4) autonomous commercial motor vehicles (CMV AVs). Surface transportation authorization expires September 30, 2026, forcing Congress to reconcile a fragmented state-by-state regulatory patchwork with the operational realities of interstate autonomous trucking [22][7]. Simultaneously, the European Union's UNECE-aligned type-approval regime imposes a structurally different pre-market certification pathway, creating measurable transatlantic divergence in deployment velocity, liability allocation, and workforce transition profiles [3].

## Key Systems Under Analysis

**United States — BUILD America 250 Act (H.R. 8870).** Advanced by the House Transportation & Infrastructure Committee on May 22, 2026, by a 62–2 bipartisan vote, this $580 billion reauthorization embeds — for the first time — a federal regulatory framework for CMV AVs operating in interstate commerce [22]. The framework pivots from state-level experimentation toward a unified federal oversight model, developed from over 11,000 solicited policy inputs [7].

**European Union — UNECE Type-Approval Framework.** Europe mandates Europe-wide type approval (or at minimum national approval) *prior* to market introduction or large-scale field testing of automated vehicles [3]. This ex-ante certification approach contrasts sharply with the U.S. ex-post, operations-oriented framework, producing distinct safety-impact evaluation challenges — retrospective assessment of ADS collision-prevention effectiveness remains methodologically immature, with no established best practices [3].
